item_description: Suzi Quatro Black leather jumpsuit
caption: 1 Suzi Quatro Gibson EBO bass guitar Gold leather jumpsuit and boots American singer-songwriter Suzi Quatro moved to the UK in 1971 after being discovered in hometown Detroit by manager Mickie Most. She was one of the first women to break the mould and play glam rock. For the 1973 performance of her first UK No.1 ‘Can The Can’ on Top of the Pops, Quatro was inspired by Elvis’ 68 Comeback Special and requested to wear leather. Most suggested a leather jumpsuit, which joined her bass guitar to create her distinctive image. By kind permission of Suzi Quatro

item_description: Do They Know It's Christmas Single and Picture Disc
item_title: Do They Know It's Christmas Single and Picture Disc
music_artists: Band Aid | Bob Geldof | Midge Ure | Peter Blake
caption: 1 Band Aid ‘Do They Know It’s Christmas?’ Single and Picture Disc Following a BBC News report highlighting a famine in Ethiopia, Bob Geldof formed Band Aid - a super-group to record a charity single.  ‘Do They Know It’s Christmas?’ was co-written by Geldof and Midge Ure and the sleeve was designed by Sir Peter Blake. It was recorded on the 25th November 1984 and released just four days later in time for Christmas. The record went straight to number one, became the biggest selling record in chart history and raised over £8,000,000 for the relief effort.

item_description: Bob Geldof Band Aid T-Shirt
caption: 2 Bob Geldof Band Aid T-Shirt This T-Shirt was designed and worn by Bob Geldof during the recording of ‘Do They Know It’s Christmas?’ in 1984. The simple yet powerful slogan ‘Feed The World’ was drawn from the lyrics and was the call to arms to raise money for the Ethiopian famine. The T-Shirt would become a classic design and form part of a range of merchandise, including posters and calendars, raising money for the famine relief.

caption: 6 Take That dolls and ephemera Boyzone fan club ephemera Spice Girls dolls and fan club ephemera The mid-1990s saw an increase in boy and girl bands targeted at the youth market. This attracted a range of merchandise on a scale unseen since the days of The Beatles in the 1960s. All manner of items - from toy dolls and sticker books to bed linen and scarves - were produced to meet the rising demand for band-related goods from fans. This lucrative and marketable business tailed off with the break-up of Take That and the Spice Girls (the first time round) in the late 1990s.

item_title: Bass guitar played by Bill Wyman
caption: 4 The Rolling Stones Bass guitar played by Bill Wyman Bill Wyman joined R&B band The Rolling Stones on bass guitar in 1962 as a replacement for Dick Taylor. He had previously been touring his own invention – the fretless bass - with his band The Cliftons on the London circuit. Impressing the group with his ability on guitar, the instrument itself and his vocals, Wyman sailed through The Rolling Stones audition. His ‘walking bass’ style of playing coupled with Charlie Watts’ drumming provided the distinctive pulsating sound behind a number of their hits. This Dan Armstrong bass guitar has a short scale sliding pick up and was played by Wyman on the 1975 and 1978 US tours. By kind permission of Bill Wyman’s Personal Archive

item_description: Freddie Mercury trousers and jacket
Sixpence plectrum
caption: 6 Queen ‘John Birch’ electric guitar and amp played by Brian May The first and probably most talked-about replica of Brian’s home made guitar, affectionately known as the Red Special, is simply called ‘the John Birch’. It was the main live backup to the Red Special during the late 1970s/early 1980s and famously appeared in Queen’s We Will Rock You and Spread Your Wings video shoots in 1977, before meeting an ignominious end at a show in New Jersey in 1982. “I wasn’t somebody who habitually smashed up his guitar or set alight to it, but there was one night, where I had broken a string and I had picked up a spare, which was the John Birch replica of my guitar, a pale brown-coloured Red Special, and the thing just didn’t cooperate – it wouldn’t play properly – I couldn’t get any sound out of it. It didn’t seem to be close to in tune and it sounded like a wet blanket to me; so in total frustration I lobbed it up in the air and had no idea where it would land.” Brian May In 2004, the guitar was rediscovered in bits and shipped back to Brian and repaired by Andrew Guyton Brian May would play the guitar with a Vox AC30 amplifier distorting at full power. This, combined with his unusual choice of a sixpence as a plectrum, helped to create his legendary guitar sound. By kind permission of Brian May
